turns.content: I'm in my late 20s and I feel like I should be doing more with my money. Where do I start?
The classic sequence: emergency fund first (3–6 months of expenses), then pay off high-interest debt, then invest. Most people do these out of order and it costs them.
Anything above roughly 6–7% — credit cards are the main culprit. Below that, the math usually favors investing over paying down debt aggressively.
Should I prioritize my 401k or paying off student loans?
Get the full employer match first — that's a 50–100% instant return on your contribution. Then evaluate the loan interest rate against expected market returns.
What should I invest in inside my 401k?
At your age, a low-cost total stock market index fund or a target-date fund matching your retirement year. Vanguard, Fidelity, and Schwab all offer excellent options with very low expense ratios.
What is an expense ratio and why does it matter?
It's the annual fee the fund charges, expressed as a percentage. 0.03% vs 1% sounds tiny but compounds dramatically over 30 years — it can mean the difference of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Should I also have a Roth IRA?
If you're under the income limit (roughly $146K single for 2024), yes — contribute to a Roth IRA after getting the 401k match. Tax-free growth on that money for 30+ years is extremely valuable.
Is a financial advisor worth it?
For most people in their 20s with straightforward finances, a fee-only advisor for a one-time review can be valuable. Avoid commission-based advisors — their incentives aren't aligned with yours.
What's the one habit that makes the biggest difference?
Automating your savings so the money never hits your checking account. Pay yourself first, then live on what's left. Willpower is finite; automation is not.
